R06-E-01: Public health suffers from a peculiar handicap: when it succeeds, nothing happens. A hospital can display the patients it has cured and a surgeon can point to the tumour she removed, but the officials who ran a vaccination campaign have nothing to show for their work except an absence. The measles outbreak that did not occur leaves no photographs, no grateful survivors and no line in the local newspaper. Success in prevention is a count of events that never took place, and such a count is always an estimate rather than an observation. This invisibility is more than an inconvenience for those who would like credit. It changes how the public weighs risk. When a disease has been made rare, the vaccine against it becomes more noticeable than the disease itself. A parent who has never seen a child struggle to breathe with diphtheria, but who has heard about a neighbour's child running a fever after an injection, is weighing something vivid against something abstract. From where that parent stands, the calculation is not foolish; the danger really has receded from ordinary experience. What the parent may not see is that it receded because of the very programme now being doubted, and that it can return if enough people reach the same conclusion. The same pattern appears wherever the benefit of a measure is an event that fails to happen. A food inspection service that keeps contaminated products off the shelves is easy to cut in a lean year, because the year after the cut looks much like the year before it. The costs of neglect arrive slowly, are spread thinly, and are usually blamed on something else by the time they become visible. Spending on treatment, by contrast, answers a need that is present and named. It is not surprising that budgets drift towards cure and away from prevention even when prevention is the cheaper way to buy the same health. None of this means that the public should simply take officials at their word. Claims about disasters averted are claims about a world that did not happen, and they can be inflated by any agency that wants to protect its budget. The answer to invisibility is not deference but better ways of making the counterfactual visible: comparisons with places and periods that lacked the measure, honest accounting of the measure's own costs and side effects, and records kept carefully enough that a sceptic could check them. Prevention will never be as photogenic as rescue, but it can be made legible, and a public that can read its record is more likely to keep paying for it.
R06-E-02: Few health instructions are repeated as confidently as the one about sleep: adults need about eight hours, and those hours should come in a single unbroken block. Someone who wakes at three in the morning and lies awake for an hour is likely to describe the experience as a disorder, and to spend the next day worrying about it. Advice is sought, remedies are bought, and an hour of wakefulness becomes a problem to be solved. Yet the second half of that instruction, the part about continuity, has a shorter history than its confidence suggests. Historians reading diaries, legal testimony and household advice from pre-industrial Europe have noticed casual references to a 'first sleep' and a 'second sleep', separated by a spell of wakefulness in the middle of the night. People used that interval to pray, tend the fire, talk quietly, or simply lie in the dark and think. What is striking about these references is not their content but their tone: the waking interval is mentioned as an ordinary feature of the night, not as a complaint. One explanation offered for its later disappearance is the spread of cheap artificial light, which pushed bedtimes later and compressed the night into a single shorter stretch, though the evidence for this is suggestive rather than conclusive. If consolidated sleep is partly a product of custom, then some of what is now labelled insomnia may be a mismatch between a person and a norm rather than a fault in the person. This matters because worry about sleep is itself a powerful disrupter of sleep. A person who wakes in the night and concludes that something has gone wrong becomes more alert, and stays awake longer, than one who regards the waking as unremarkable. The norm, in other words, can help produce the very failures it is used to diagnose. It would be a mistake, however, to replace one myth with another. The historical record does not show that segmented sleep is the true human pattern from which industrial society has led us astray; it shows that sleep has taken more than one form, depending on light, work and season. Nor does any of this make chronic sleep loss harmless. People who sleep too little over long periods do suffer for it, and some sleep complaints call for medical attention. The modest lesson is that a description of how many people sleep should not be mistaken for a rule about how everyone must.
R06-E-03: In the design of a clinical trial, the placebo plays the role of nothing. Patients in one group receive the drug, patients in the other receive an inert imitation, and whatever improvement the second group shows is subtracted from the first as background noise. The logic is sound for its purpose, which is to establish whether a molecule does anything beyond the act of being given. But the habit of treating the placebo arm as a measure of nothing has encouraged a further and less defensible assumption, that the improvement seen there is not real, or at least not interesting. It is both. What patients in a placebo group respond to is not the sugar in the pill but everything that surrounds it: the consultation, the explanation, the expectation of relief, the ritual of taking something at set hours, the attention of people whose job is to help. Some researchers prefer to speak of a 'meaning response' for this reason, since the inert pill is merely the occasion on which the meaning of being treated is delivered. On this view the placebo arm is not a blank but a measurement of how much the context of care can do by itself. The standard objection to using such effects deliberately has been ethical. A placebo, it was assumed, works only if the patient is deceived, and deceiving patients violates the trust on which medicine depends. Several small trials have unsettled this assumption by giving patients pills that were openly described as inert and still recording improvements in symptoms that the patients reported themselves. The findings are preliminary, and it is not clear how much of the effect survives once the novelty of an unusual study wears off. Even so, they suggest that deception may be less essential to the response than was believed, and that the ritual may matter more than the belief that the pill is active. Enthusiasts are quick to go further than the evidence allows. Responses to placebo are most consistent for symptoms that are experienced and reported, such as pain, nausea and fatigue; there is little reason to think that the meaning of a consultation can shrink a tumour or clear an infection. The more useful conclusion is not that doctors should prescribe sugar pills but that the manner of care is itself a part of treatment. A health system that shortens consultations to save money may be removing an active ingredient without ever recording the loss, because its effect was always filed under nothing.
R06-E-04: Discussions of antibiotic resistance usually begin with misuse: drugs prescribed for viral infections that they cannot touch, courses abandoned halfway, animals dosed to make them grow faster. Each of these practices gives bacteria more opportunities to evolve defences, and each deserves the attention it receives. Less often discussed is a quieter problem that has nothing to do with carelessness. Even if every prescription were perfectly judged, the way new antibiotics are paid for would discourage anyone from making them. Consider what responsible use of a genuinely new antibiotic would look like. Because every use exerts selective pressure, the new drug should be held back for patients whose infections resist older and cheaper treatments, and it should be prescribed as rarely as possible for as long as possible. This is sound medicine. It is also a commercial disaster. A company recovers the cost of developing a drug by selling it in quantity during the years its patent protects it, and a drug that doctors are urged not to use cannot be sold in quantity. The contrast with a medicine for a chronic condition, taken every day for decades by millions of people, could hardly be sharper. It is not surprising that large firms have drifted out of the field, or that small firms that have brought new antibiotics through approval have sometimes failed commercially soon afterwards. The proposed remedy is to separate a company's income from the number of doses it sells. Under such schemes, a health system would pay a fixed annual sum for access to a new antibiotic, whether it is used on a thousand patients or on ten, much as a town pays for a fire brigade whether or not anything burns that year. The payment rewards the existence of the drug rather than its consumption, which is exactly the property a reserve antibiotic is supposed to have. The objections are real. Such payments are large, they must be justified to budget holders who see little use for their money, and nobody knows quite how to price a drug whose value lies mainly in emergencies it may never have to meet. Nor would better payment by itself guarantee discovery, since finding compounds that kill resistant bacteria without harming patients is scientifically hard. But these difficulties argue for designing the schemes carefully, not for abandoning them. The alternative is to go on rewarding a pattern of sales that good medicine forbids, and to discover the cost only when the older drugs have stopped working.
R06-E-05: For most of the twentieth century, medicine described its relationship with microbes in the language of war. Bacteria invaded, the immune system defended, and antibiotics were weapons that wiped out the enemy. The metaphor was not idle decoration. It organised research around identifying a single culprit for each disease and finding a means of killing it, and that programme saved an enormous number of lives. The study of the microbes that live in and on healthy bodies has made the war metaphor look crude. Most of these organisms are not enemies; many are useful, helping to digest food, train the immune system and occupy space that harmful species would otherwise take. An ecological vocabulary has therefore become popular: the body is a habitat, the gut is a crowded ecosystem, and health is a matter of the right community rather than the absence of germs. This vocabulary explains things the older one could not. It makes sense of why a broad course of antibiotics can be followed by a stubborn intestinal infection: by clearing out the resident species, the drug removes the competitors that had kept a harmful one in check. It also makes sense of why transferring gut bacteria from a healthy donor has proved effective against that very infection. Yet the new metaphor carries risks of its own, and they are less often noticed because it sounds so benign. Ecology, popularly understood, suggests balance and harmony, as though every body had a single proper community to which it should be restored. Ecologists themselves are more cautious; real ecosystems have many stable states, change with season and disturbance, and do not come with a correct composition. The popular version has proved ideal for marketing. Products that promise to 'rebalance' the gut can borrow the authority of a serious science while specifying nothing that could be measured, and the vagueness of the promise protects it from ever being shown false. The lesson is not that medicine should return to the language of war, nor that metaphors can be avoided. Every science thinks partly through images, and the choice is between images that sharpen questions and images that blur them. The ecological picture is valuable when it brings with it the working concepts of ecology, such as competition, succession and the effects of disturbance, which generate predictions that can be tested. It becomes a liability when it brings only the mood of ecology, a feeling of harmony that no experiment could ever contradict.
R06-E-06: The ordinary picture of pain is that of a gauge. Tissue is damaged, nerves carry a report of the damage to the brain, and the strength of the pain reflects the size of the injury, much as the needle on a dial reflects the pressure in a pipe. The picture is intuitive and, for a great many everyday injuries, roughly accurate. A burnt finger hurts more than a scratched one, and both stop hurting as they heal. The difficulty is that the gauge picture fails precisely where pain matters most. People sometimes suffer serious wounds in moments of danger or intense concentration and feel little until the moment has passed. Others feel vivid pain in limbs that have been amputated, where there is no tissue left to report anything. Most troubling of all, a large number of people continue to hurt for months or years after an injury has, by every available measure, healed. If pain were a reading of damage, none of this should happen. A pressure gauge that behaved in these ways would simply be sent back for repair. An alternative account treats pain not as a reading but as a verdict. Signals from the tissues are one input among several; the brain combines them with context, expectation and memory, and produces pain when it concludes that the body is under threat and needs protecting. On this account, the soldier who feels nothing has a brain occupied with a greater threat, the amputee's brain is responding to a map of a body part that persists after the part is gone, and long-lasting pain may reflect a protective system that has grown oversensitive, raising the alarm long after the danger has passed. This account is sometimes heard as a polite way of saying that the pain is imaginary, and patients with long-standing pain have good reason to be wary of anything that sounds like that. But the claim is the reverse. A verdict produced by the nervous system is as real as any other bodily event, and it hurts just as much. What changes is where treatment might be aimed. If the alarm itself has become oversensitive, then searching ever harder for a damaged structure, and operating on whatever turns up in a scan, may do little good, while approaches that address the protective system as a whole, through explanation, graded activity and attention to fear, may help where repairs to the tissues did not.
R06-E-07: Few medical ideas seem as self-evidently right as early detection. A disease found sooner is a disease treated sooner, and a disease treated sooner, surely, is more often cured. Screening programmes, which look for disease in people who feel perfectly well, are built on this reasoning, and the figures they produce appear to confirm it. People whose cancers are found by screening typically survive far longer after diagnosis than people whose cancers are found because they caused symptoms. Patients who have been through screening often say as much, and public campaigns repeat the message with understandable conviction. It is hard to imagine clearer evidence that looking early pays. The trouble is that the comparison is rigged, though by the arithmetic of detection rather than by anyone's intent. Suppose a tumour will kill a woman at seventy whatever is done. If it causes symptoms at sixty-eight, she survives two years after diagnosis; if a scan finds it at sixty-three, she survives seven. Nothing about her death has changed, but the survival figure has more than tripled, simply because the clock was started earlier. A second distortion arises from the different speeds at which tumours grow. A test repeated every few years is far more likely to catch a slow tumour, which lingers in a detectable but harmless state for a long time, than a fast one, which may appear and cause symptoms between two tests. Screened groups are therefore loaded with the gentler cases, and their better survival partly reflects what was found rather than what was done. The most uncomfortable distortion takes this tendency to its limit. Some of the abnormalities found by screening, though they look like cancer under the microscope, would never have grown enough to cause harm in the person's lifetime. Detecting them is called overdiagnosis, and it is not an error in the usual sense, since the cells are what the pathologist says they are. The error lies in the prediction that they would have mattered, and since such a lesion is removed or destroyed once it is found, the prediction is never put to the test. People with such findings are treated, sometimes with surgery or radiation, and they then appear in the statistics as survivors, which of course they are, though they were never in danger. Because no individual can know that his or her own tumour was of this harmless kind, every overdiagnosed patient experiences the treatment as a rescue. Screening thus produces its own most sincere advocates, and the more it overdiagnoses, the more grateful survivors it creates. None of this shows that screening is useless. For some cancers, carefully conducted trials comparing large screened and unscreened populations have found fewer deaths among those screened, and those programmes deserve their place. The point concerns the evidence, not the verdict. The question to ask of a screening programme is not how long its patients live after diagnosis but whether fewer people in the population it serves die of the disease, and whether that benefit outweighs the harm of treating people who were never going to be ill. Survival after diagnosis cannot answer that question, because it improves under the influence of lead time, slow tumours and overdiagnosis even when not a single death has been prevented. Doctors are not immune to the appeal of the survival figure, since it describes the patients they actually see; the deaths a programme fails to prevent, and the needless treatments it imposes, are visible only in comparisons between whole populations that no single clinic can make.
R06-E-08: A randomised trial, for all its authority, answers a question about groups. It tells us that among patients like those enrolled, the people given a treatment did better on average than the people who were not, by an amount that can be estimated with known uncertainty. The doctor in a consulting room faces a different question, about a single person, and the gap between the two questions has produced two opposite errors, each of which presents itself as wisdom. The first error is to apply the average as though it were a fact about each patient. If a drug lowers the risk of a stroke over five years from ten in a hundred to seven in a hundred, it is tempting to say that it reduces every patient's risk by three points. But the trial cannot show this. The same average would result if a small minority benefited a great deal and everyone else not at all, or if many benefited modestly while a few were harmed. An average is a summary of a distribution, and very different distributions share the same summary. Even afterwards the matter stays hidden: a patient who takes the drug and has no stroke cannot tell whether the drug or good fortune spared him. To promise a particular patient a reduction of three points is to claim knowledge the trial does not contain. The second error starts from this observation and draws the wrong conclusion. Since every patient is different, it says, trial results do not apply to the person in front of me, and I must rely on my clinical judgement. The premise is true and the conclusion does not follow. That patients differ is not news; what matters is whether they differ in ways that change how they respond to this treatment, and the clinician's impression is a poor instrument for discovering that. A doctor's experience is itself a kind of trial, but one without randomisation, with a small sample, no comparison group and a memory that favours vivid cases. If a large trial cannot reveal who benefits, a recollection of a few dozen patients is unlikely to do better. Nor is the obvious remedy, examining subgroups within the trial, as reliable as it appears. Divide a trial's patients by age, sex, severity and a dozen other features, and some subgroups will show striking benefit or none at all purely by chance; the more divisions are made, the more such mirages appear. Findings of this kind have often failed to reappear when tested again. This does not mean that genuine differences in response do not exist. It means that claims about them need evidence as demanding as the evidence for the average itself, such as a plausible mechanism together with a difference that recurs in a fresh trial. What follows is neither the tyranny of the average nor the licence of intuition. The average is the best default available when nothing more is known, and departures from it should be justified by reasons rather than by a sense that this patient is special. For some chronic conditions whose symptoms come and go quickly, it is even possible to run a trial within a single patient, alternating the treatment with a placebo over several periods and comparing the results. Such designs are not always practical, but they show what an answer to the individual question would actually require, and how little the bare assertion of individuality provides.
